analysis.one_liner: Lets workers who face intentional job discrimination recover compensatory and punitive damages from employers.
analysis.headline: Passed the Senate 93-5 and the House 381-38 and was signed into law on November 21, 1991, as Public Law 102-166.
analysis.plain_summary: This law restored and strengthened remedies for victims of workplace discrimination after a 1989 Supreme Court decision made those cases harder to win. It lets workers who prove intentional discrimination recover money for emotional harm and, where there is malice or reckless indifference, punitive damages — capped by employer size. It also set rules for cases where a facially neutral practice has discriminatory effects, applied civil rights protections to congressional employees for the first time, and created a commission to study barriers to women and minorities advancing into management.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience intentional discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or disability can now recover compensatory damages for actual harm and, where malice or reckless indifference is shown, punitive damages [S2][S3]. Plaintiffs get the right to a jury trial when seeking these damages, and attorneys' fees and expert fees if they win [S2][S3]. Workers harmed by employment practices with discriminatory effects get defined standards of proof replacing the court-imposed burden from the Wards Cove decision [S2][S3]. Federal employees get a longer window to sue after an adverse decision, and congressional employees get civil rights protections enforced through new Senate and House procedures [S2][S3]. Women and minorities gain from the new Glass Ceiling Commission study of barriers to advancement [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Allows compensatory and punitive damages for intentional employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or disability — money for actual harm beyond back pay.

Defines standards of proof for disparate-impact cases, re-establishing protections after the 1989 Wards Cove ruling had shifted the burden to workers to prove an employer had no business justification.
Gives any party the right to a jury trial when compensatory or punitive damages are sought, and allows attorney's fees and expert fees for prevailing parties.
Applies federal civil rights protections to employees of the Senate, the House, and congressional agencies for the first time, creating the Office of Senate Fair Employment Practices.
Creates the Glass Ceiling Commission to study and recommend ways to remove barriers keeping women and minorities out of management positions.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination pay compensatory and punitive damages on top of back pay; the amounts are capped based on the size of the employer's workforce, and punitive damages are not available against governments [S3]. Businesses also bear the litigation costs of a right to a jury trial in damages cases [S2]. Employers cannot block claims merely by showing a practice is a 'business necessity' when the claim is intentional discrimination [S3].

drawbacks.text: Damages are capped at amounts that vary by employer size, so victims of discrimination at large companies recover less than a jury might award — and the jury is not even told the caps exist, limiting informed factfinding.

No compensatory or punitive damages are available in disparate-impact cases or against government employers, and none for back pay or equitable relief, leaving some serious discrimination without a full money remedy.

The ban on adjusting test scores by race or sex (so-called race-norming) was opposed by civil rights advocates who argued it eliminated an affirmative tool for integrating workforces; the bill declares such score adjustment unlawful.

Discrimination claims by Senate employees are handled inside the Senate itself, through its own fair employment office and Ethics Committee, with enforcement in the Senate's exclusive jurisdiction rather than ordinary courts — protections Congress applied to others but kept partially in its own hands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: for the first time, victims of intentional job discrimination can recover meaningful money damages, which gives employers a direct financial reason not to discriminate. The main costs fall on employers in litigation and verdicts, but the negotiated caps on damages — scaled to company size — were the compromise that brought business groups and the White House along, so the burden was deliberately moderated. The worst flaw is that Congress enforced civil rights protections on its own staff through internal Senate and House procedures instead of the regular courts.

outcome.mechanism: It sailed through both chambers in weeks — the Senate 93-5, the House 381-38 — after a negotiated compromise, and the President signed it on November 21, 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced September 24, 1991 by Senator John Danforth, a Republican from Missouri, with six Republican cosponsors; the Senate placed it on its calendar the same day.

In early October, opponents tried to keep the bill from reaching the floor — motions to proceed were made and withdrawn and cloture motions were filed on October 7 and October 17 — before cloture was invoked on October 22 by 93-4, with all 55 voting Democrats in favor and 38 of 43 Republicans in favor.
An attempt to block the bill on a point of order failed badly on October 29, 22-76, after which the Senate adopted the substitute as amended and passed the bill 93-5 on October 30.
The House took it up November 7 under a rule that allowed one motion to commit and no amendments, and passed it 381-38 — Democrats 252-5, Republicans 128-33.
The President signed it November 21, 1991, and it became Public Law 102-166.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who face discrimination are better off: they gained the right to collect compensatory and punitive damages that did not exist before. Employers accepted the deal because the negotiated damage caps limited their worst-case exposure, which is also why the bill rather than a stronger version became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Discrimination victims, and employers with capped liability

for.name: Sen. John C. Danforth
for.role: Lead Republican sponsor and chief Senate negotiator
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1745 on September 24, 1991 and shepherded it through the Senate to passage 93-5.

for.name: 93 senators (55 of 57 Democrats, 38 of 43 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Voted to open debate and passed the bill 93-5 on October 30, 1991.

for.name: 381 House members (252 of 266 Democrats, 128 of 165 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Passed the Senate bill without amendment, 381-38, on November 7, 1991.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on November 21, 1991 as Public Law 102-166.

for.name: Civil rights coalition (Leadership Conference on Civil Rights and allied groups)
for.what_they_did: Pressured Congress for two years to reverse the 1989 Wards Cove decision and restore discrimination remedies after the 1990 version was vetoed; backed the 1991 compromise.

for.name: Business groups (Business Roundtable, U.S. Chamber of Commerce)
for.what_they_did: Initially opposed uncapped damages, then negotiated the compromise — accepting damages with caps — that allowed the bill to pass and be signed.

against.name: 38 House members (33 of 165 Republicans, 5 of 266 Democrats)
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage on November 7, 1991.

against.name: 5 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage 93-5 on October 30, 1991.

against.name: 22 senators (6 of 57 Democrats, 16 of 43 Republicans)
against.what_they_did: Voted on October 29, 1991 to sustain a point of order against the bill; the effort failed 22-76.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: Senate Democrats backed it 55-0 and Republicans 38-5; House Democrats 252-5 and Republicans 128-33, with the main opponents a small bloc of Republicans.

industries.note: Employers that intentionally discriminate can now be ordered to pay compensatory and punitive damages on top of back pay, with jury trials available. The caps scaled to workforce size limit the exposure, which is why business groups ultimately accepted the deal rather than fighting it.

The law extended civil rights protections to congressional employees for the first time, but gave the Senate its own fair employment office and kept enforcement in the Senate's exclusive jurisdiction, with the Ethics Committee retaining disciplinary power — Congress regulated itself through its own channels rather than ordinary courts.
Punitive damages are not available against government employers, shielding public employers from the harshest category of damages that private employers face.
